title: How to Use a Garlic Press for Quick Garlic Confit Paste
meta_description: Learn how to use a garlic press for garlic confit to create a rich, spreadable paste in half the time. Easy steps for a chef-quality kitchen staple.
html:
Most people think of a garlic press as a tool for quick sautéing or adding a punch to a salad dressing. But if you've ever struggled with the tedious task of finely dicing garlic for a confit, you know that the prep work can be the most daunting part. Using a garlic press for garlic confit is a game-changer. Instead of spending twenty minutes with a chef's knife, you can create a uniform, jammy paste that infuses oil more deeply and spreads more easily than whole cloves.

Garlic confit—slow-cooking garlic in oil—is a kitchen luxury. It transforms pungent, sharp raw cloves into sweet, mellow gold. By pressing the garlic first, you increase the surface area, allowing the oil to penetrate the garlic more efficiently and resulting in a luxurious paste that is perfect for toast, roasted meats, or mixing into mashed potatoes.

Why Use a Garlic Press for Garlic Confit?

When you slow-roast whole cloves, you get soft, individual pieces. That's great for some dishes, but for a versatile condiment, a paste is superior. Manually mincing garlic to a paste consistency requires a lot of effort and a very sharp knife. A Garlic Press allows you to achieve that consistency in seconds.

Because the Garlic Press is made of sturdy stainless steel and silicone, it handles the pressure of multiple cloves without bending. The result is a consistent mash that cooks evenly. Since the garlic is already broken down, the heat from the oil softens the fibers faster, reducing your overall stovetop or oven time while intensifying the flavor infusion.

Ingredients and Tools You'll Need

To get started, keep your ingredient list simple. The quality of the oil is where you can really elevate the dish. I recommend a high-quality extra virgin olive oil or a neutral grapeseed oil if you want the garlic flavor to be the sole star.

  • 3-4 whole heads of garlic (peeled)
  • 2 cups of olive oil (enough to fully submerge the garlic)
  • A pinch of kosher salt
  • Fresh thyme or a bay leaf (optional, for aroma)
  • Our Garlic Press for prepping the cloves
  • A small oven-safe ramekin or a heavy-bottomed saucepan

Step-by-Step: Making the Garlic Confit Paste

The secret to a great confit is low and slow heat. If the oil gets too hot, the garlic will brown and turn bitter. Here is the most efficient way to use your garlic press for garlic confit paste.

First, peel your garlic cloves. While some presses handle unpeeled cloves, peeling them first ensures a smoother paste and prevents any stray papery skins from ending up in your oil. Use the Garlic Press to crush the cloves directly into your cooking vessel. Work in batches, squeezing the garlic until you have a thick mound of minced garlic in the pot.

Pour the olive oil over the pressed garlic. The oil should cover the garlic by at least an inch. Add your salt and any herbs. If you are using an oven, set it to 250°F (120°C) and bake for about 45 to 60 minutes. If you are using the stovetop, keep it on the lowest possible simmer. You aren't looking for bubbles; you're looking for a very gentle warmth.

Once the garlic is a pale golden color and feels soft when pressed with a fork, remove it from the heat. The oil will now be infused with a deep, nutty garlic aroma, and the solids will have the consistency of a spreadable butter.

Storage and Safety Tips

Because garlic in oil creates an anaerobic environment (meaning no oxygen), it can be a risk for botulism if stored incorrectly at room temperature. To keep your confit safe, always transfer it to a sterilized glass jar and store it in the refrigerator immediately after it cools.

Your garlic confit paste will stay fresh in the fridge for about two weeks. For longer storage, I recommend freezing the paste in ice cube trays. Once frozen, pop the cubes into a freezer bag. You can drop a single cube of garlic confit directly into a pan for a quick pasta sauce or a sauté, saving you from having to reach for the Garlic Press every single time you cook.

Ways to Use Your Garlic Confit Paste

Now that you've mastered using a garlic press for garlic confit, the possibilities are endless. Start by spreading a thick layer on toasted sourdough and topping it with a poached egg. The mellow sweetness of the confit balances the richness of the yolk perfectly.

You can also stir a spoonful into mayonnaise for the ultimate aioli, or fold it into butter to make a compound butter for steak. Even the leftover oil is liquid gold—use it to sear vegetables or drizzle over a bowl of creamy polenta. The versatility of the paste makes the few minutes spent with the Garlic Press well worth the effort.

FAQ

Can I use a garlic press with unpeeled cloves for confit?

While some high-end presses can handle skins, it is better to peel the cloves first. This ensures the paste is smooth and prevents bitter bits of skin from being infused into your oil during the slow-cooking process.

Why is my garlic confit turning dark brown?

If the garlic turns dark brown or black, the heat was too high. Confit should be a pale gold. If it browns too quickly, the flavor becomes acrid rather than sweet. Lower your oven temperature or turn your burner to the absolute lowest setting.

Is a garlic press better than chopping for this recipe?

Yes, for a paste consistency. Chopping can get you close, but a Garlic Press breaks down the cellular structure of the garlic more effectively, leading to a more uniform texture and a faster infusion of flavor into the oil.
